transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my wife... she's the one who made the appointment. I haven't been working, so I'm just at the house all day, and I guess things have just been really heavy lately. But what really pushed her over the edge, what finally scared her enough to drag me down here, is what’s been happening with the walls. 

I keep hearing these sounds. It started with just water, like water running inside the pipes, but we don't have any leaks. I went down to the basement, I checked the valves, I checked everything. And then... it’s not just water anymore. I hear men whispering. Right inside the drywall. Just these low, muffled voices, whispering back and forth when I know for a fact nobody else is in the house. I'll press my ear right up against the plaster in the living room and it's like they're right there, just out of sight. 

And then, the hallway... sometimes I look down it and I see this... this dark, wet patch. Just spreading across the floorboards. Like a stain, creeping out. And I'll go get a towel, I'll go right up to it and touch it to wipe it up, and it's completely dry. There's nothing there. I can feel the dry wood, but I still see it spreading. I try to explain it to my wife, how real it is, but she just gets this terrified look on her face. She told me I had to come talk to someone because she doesn't know what to do with me anymore. I just... I don't understand how it can be dry when I'm looking right at it.
How long have you been hearing these whispers and seeing the dark patch in the hallway?

Well, it's... it's been a while now. I'd say about seven months. It started back during the winter freeze, you know, when the pipes actually did freeze up on us. It was such a nightmare. The whole house was just freezing cold, and I was trying to fix the insulation, trying to wrap the pipes, but it was just... it was too much. I couldn't keep up with the repairs, and the house just felt like it was falling apart around me. It was this huge mess that I just couldn't get out from under, no matter how hard I tried. 

And that's when the sounds started. Right around then. At first, I thought it was just the ice melting, you know, the water finally moving through the pipes again after the freeze. I'd sit there in the living room, wrapped in a blanket, just listening to it. But then the freeze ended, and the sounds didn't stop. They just changed. That's when the water turned into the whispering. And the dark patch in the hallway... that started a little bit after, maybe a few weeks later. I thought maybe a pipe had burst and I just couldn't find the leak, but like I said, it's always dry. It's been seven months of this, day in and day out, and I just... I don't know how much more I can take. It's like the house is alive, and it's just... it's just waiting for me.
Was there anything unusual or particularly stressful happening in your life around the time the winter freeze occurred and the sounds started?

Well, I mean, the freeze itself was just... it was catastrophic. We had that massive storm, the one that knocked the power out for three days, and I was already... I was already just so down. I had lost my job a few months before that, back in the fall. They downsized the whole department, just wiped us out, and I had been trying to find something else, sending out resumes, making calls, but nobody was biting. And it just started to wear on me, you know? I stopped getting out of bed before noon, stopped shaving, stopped even caring if I found a job. I just felt like this massive failure, like I couldn't provide for my wife, couldn't even keep my own life together. 

So by the time the freeze hit, I was already in this really dark place. I was just sitting in the house all day, staring at the walls, feeling like I was drowning in this... this heaviness. It was like I was already dead and just waiting for my body to catch up. And then the pipes froze, and it was just the straw that broke the camel's back. I couldn't even keep my own house warm. 

But the thing is, before all that... before I lost my job and got so incredibly down, before I stopped caring about everything and just felt like a complete and utter failure every single day... I never had any of this other stuff happen. I never heard any voices in the drywall, I never saw those creeping wet patches in the hallway that turn out to be completely dry, and I definitely never thought the neighbors were, you know, keeping tabs on me or tracking my movements or anything like that. All of that... the whispers, the stains, the feeling like I'm being watched... that only started happening after I was already deep, deep into this... this hole. It was like the house sensed how broken I was and just started reflecting it back at me. It didn't start until I had already given up.
Do you think the whispers you hear in the walls are trying to convey any specific messages to you or about you?

Well, the messages... it's hard to make out exactly what they're saying, word for word, because it's always that low, muffled sound, like they're trying not to be overheard. But I know what it's about. I know what they're talking about. It's... it's the house itself. The mold, the wiring... I know it sounds crazy, I know it sounds completely far-fetched, but I am absolutely certain that the mold and the old wiring in that house have just... poisoned everything. It's seeped into everything I own, all my clothes, the furniture, the air we breathe. It's like this toxic rot that's just contaminating my whole life. 

And the whispers, they're talking about it. They're talking about how ruined everything is, how I let it get this way. And it's not just the voices in the walls, either. I can tell... I can just tell that the neighbors know. I see them looking at the house, looking at me when I go out to get the mail. They're watching. They're watching to see when I'm going to mess up again, when I'm finally going to just completely collapse under the weight of it all. They know I can't fix it, they know I'm a failure, and they're just waiting for the final shoe to drop. It's all connected—the poison in the house, the whispering, the neighbors watching me. It's all just closing in on me, day after day, and I can't scrub it clean. No matter how much I try to wipe up that dry patch, no matter how much I check the pipes... the poison is just there, and everyone knows it.
Do you ever find it hard to organize your thoughts or express them in a way that feels coherent to you?

Well, no, not really. I mean, my thoughts are... they're fine. I know what I want to say, and I say it. It's just that there's so much to say, you know? There's so much happening all at once, and it's all so heavy. Like, when I try to explain about the house, about the mold and the way the air feels thick, I have to explain the whole thing because otherwise, it doesn't make sense. If I just say 'the house is poisoned,' people look at me like I'm crazy. But if I explain about the freeze, and the pipes, and the way the water sounded before it turned into the whispers... then they have to understand, right? 

So, I don't think my thoughts are disorganized. I think they're actually very clear. It's just that the reality of what's happening to me is so complicated. And it's exhausting, having to explain it all the time, having to make sure every detail is out there so that someone, anyone, might finally see what I'm seeing. But no, I don't lose my train of thought or get confused about what I'm trying to express. It's all very vivid. Too vivid, honestly. I just wish I didn't have to think about it at all, but it's constantly there, pressing down on me, every single minute of the day.
Have you noticed any changes in your daily behavior or activities since these whispers and visions started?

Well, it's... it's just completely taken over everything. I mean, I used to be the one who handled all the practical stuff around the house. The bills, the maintenance, making sure the gutters were cleaned out, fixing the leaky faucets... I was always on top of it. I had a system, you know? A whole spreadsheet for the finances and a schedule for the repairs. But now... I just can't. I can't even look at the mail. It piles up on the counter, these final notices with the red lettering, and I just walk right past it because it doesn't matter anymore. Nothing matters when the whole structure of your life is rotting from the inside out. 

I've stopped doing all of it. I don't fix anything, I don't pay the bills, I don't even go to the appointments I'm supposed to keep. My wife... she's had to take over everything. And it's not fair to her, I know it's not. She's working, she's trying to keep us afloat, and now she has to make all the decisions I used to handle. She's the one calling the utility companies, trying to explain why the payments are late. She's the one trying to figure out how we're going to survive this. 

And it just... it came to a head recently. The city, or the utility company, I don't even know who it was... they sent someone out for a safety inspection because of the freeze and the damage in the neighborhood. They wanted to come in, wanted to look at the pipes, look at the walls. But I couldn't let them. I knew what they were really looking for. I knew if they came in, they'd see the poison, they'd hear the whispers, they'd report it to the neighbors, and it would all just blow up. So I wouldn't let them in. I wouldn't cooperate at all. I just locked the door and sat in the hallway. It got so bad... my wife didn't know what to do with me. She ended up calling a crisis team because I was just sitting there, refusing to move, refusing to let anyone in. I just couldn't let them see how completely I've failed to protect my own home.
Do you think it's possible that the whispers and the poison in the house might not be real, or is that something you're absolutely certain about?

Well... no. No, I don't think it's possible that it's not real. I mean, I know how it sounds. I really do. If someone else came up to me and told me all of this, I'd probably think they were losing their mind. I know it sounds completely far-fetched, like something out of a bad movie, but... but I am absolutely certain. I'm certain. 

Because I can feel it, you see? It's not just a thought in my head. I can physically feel the way the mold and the old wiring in that house have just... they've poisoned everything. Everything I own. It's in the fabric of the couch, it's in the clothes hanging in the closet, it's in the very air I'm breathing. You can't just imagine something that pervasive. And it's not just the house, it's the people around it, too. I can tell... I can just feel it when I look out the window. The neighbors, they're watching. They're always watching. They stand on their porches or they peek through their blinds, and they're just waiting to see when I'm going to mess up again. They know about the poison, they know about the rot, and they're just waiting for the whole thing to collapse on top of me. 

So, no, doctor. It's not my imagination. I wish it was. God, I wish I could just wake up and find out this was all some terrible dream, but it's not. It's real. The poison, the whispers, the neighbors watching... it's all completely, undeniably real, and it's destroying everything.
Do you believe the neighbors are watching you because they want to harm you or because they are concerned about you?

Harm me? Concerned? No... no, it's not like that. It's definitely not concern. God, no. If they were actually concerned about me or my wife, they would have offered to help when the freeze happened, right? When the pipes burst. But they didn't lift a finger. They just watched. 

I know it sounds far-fetched. I really do. I hear myself talking and I know exactly how it sounds to a doctor, but... but I am absolutely certain about this. They aren't plotting to come over and physically attack me or anything like that. It's more insidious than that. They're just watching to see when I mess up again. Because they know. They know about the house. They know that the mold... that thick, creeping mold in the walls, and the old, frayed wiring that sparks when the wind blows too hard... they know it has completely poisoned everything. 

And I mean everything. It's not just a little water damage, it's a complete, total contamination of everything I own. Every piece of furniture, the rugs, the clothes in my closet... it's all steeped in this toxic rot. And the neighbors, they can sense it. They look at me like I'm the one who brought this sickness into the neighborhood. Like I'm a failure for not being able to stop it. So they just wait. They stand on their porches with their arms crossed, or they peek through those little plastic blinds—you know the ones, the cheap ones that snap when you pull them back—and they just stare at my property. 

They want to see the exact moment I completely break under the weight of it all. They want to see me drag a poisoned, ruined mattress out to the curb, or they want to see the city finally slap a condemned sticker on the front door. It's like some sick spectator sport to them. They aren't worried about my health. They just want to be there when I finally, completely fail. Because they know I can't fix the wiring. They know the mold has already won. So no, it's not concern at all. It's just... it's just this constant, heavy judgment while I'm trapped inside a house that is literally destroying me and everything I have.
Have you ever felt like you've lost touch with reality while experiencing these whispers and visions?

Lost touch with reality? I... I mean, how do you even define that when you're trapped right in the middle of it? To me, it's all happening. It's right there. But... I know my wife thinks I have. That’s actually what finally scared her so much, what really pushed her to her breaking point with all of this. 

Because I’ll be sitting there, and the house will be completely quiet—she might be reading or trying to balance the checkbook I can't look at anymore—and I can hear it. I keep hearing water running. Not just a little drip, but rushing water behind the drywall, like the pipes are just bleeding out into the insulation. And it’s not just the water. There are men whispering inside the walls. I can hear their voices, these low, murmuring voices, just talking and talking, scheming about something when I know nobody else is in the house. I try to get her to listen, I'll tell her to stop breathing so loudly and just come put her ear to the plaster, but she says there's nothing. She just looks at me with this... this terrified pity. 

And the hallway... God, the hallway is the part that really messes with my head. I’ll be walking toward the kitchen, and I will see this dark, wet patch. I watch it physically spreading across the floorboards, this toxic, dark stain just creeping out from the baseboards, getting wider and wider. It looks so wet, so undeniably real. But then... then I'll get down on my hands and knees, and I'll press my bare hand against the wood to see how bad the damage is, to feel the rot, and... it’s dry. I can see the dark stain right in front of my face, I can see the edges of it spreading, but the floor is completely, perfectly dry to the touch. 

So I don't know, doctor. I don't know if that means I've lost touch with reality or if the poison in that house is just playing tricks on me, hiding itself the second I try to prove it's there. I just know what I hear, and I know what I see. I hear the water, I hear the men, I see the dark patches spreading. And it’s terrifying my wife because she can’t experience any of it. It's just... it's exhausting. It's so incredibly exhausting to live like this every single minute of the day, never knowing why I can see the water but can't feel it.
Do you often find yourself having trouble putting your thoughts into words when trying to explain what's happening with the house?

Putting my thoughts into words... yeah. Yeah, it's... it's like trying to wade through wet cement. That's the only way I can describe it. Actually, my wife, she was just saying the other day that I move like I'm underwater now. And she's right, she really is. It’s not just that I can’t find the right words, it’s that the whole process of thinking and speaking and just existing feels so impossibly slow and heavy. 

Like, just the other day, we were trying to figure out what to do, and someone was asking me a very simple question about a repair estimate. I think it was about replacing some of the baseboards, or maybe the drywall where the water was—I don't even remember the exact details because it all just blurs together into this big, overwhelming mess of ruin. But they asked me this basic, straightforward question, something I should have been able to answer in two seconds. And I just... I stood there. I could hear the question echoing in my head, I knew I needed to answer, but getting my mouth to open and actually form the words... it took so long. 

It took so incredibly long that they just gave up. They just started talking for me. People do that a lot now. They ask me something, wait a few seconds, and then just fill in the blank themselves because I’m just standing there, staring, trying to push through this heavy, suffocating water just to get a single sentence out. It makes me feel completely useless. I mean, how can I explain what's really happening with the house, how can I make anyone understand the poison and the rot, when I can't even answer a basic question about an estimate without someone else having to step in and speak for me? It's just... it's like my brain and my body have completely ground to a halt under the weight of it all. Everything is just so slow now.
Have you felt an overwhelming sense of fear or anxiety when you think about the poison in your house?

Fear? No... no, I wouldn't use that word. Anxiety... that's not it either. I mean, anxiety is what you feel when you're waiting for the other shoe to drop, right? It’s for the 'what ifs.' Like, what if the car breaks down, or what if you lose your job. My wife, she gets anxious. She paces around the kitchen, wringing her hands, trying to figure out how to fix things that are already completely broken. But me? When I think about the poison... the mold, the contamination in everything we own... I don't feel fear. 

It’s more like... it’s just this absolute, crushing certainty. Why would I be afraid of something that has already won? You don't feel anxious when you're already drowning at the bottom of the ocean, you just feel the pressure of the water pressing down on you from all sides. That's what it is for me. Just this immense pressure. I’ll sit in my armchair—the brown recliner in the corner of the living room, the one that's probably completely soaked through with the rot by now, right down to the springs—and my heart isn't racing. I don't get sweaty palms or start panicking. I just feel... empty. And heavy. So incredibly heavy. 

I look at the walls, and I hear that water rushing behind the drywall, and I just think... well, this is it. This is what we are now. It's a complete surrender to it. Fear means you still have some kind of hope that things might turn out okay, that you can escape it. I don't have that anymore. The house is ruined, the wiring is fried, everything is steeped in this sickness. So there's no anxiety left in me. It’s all been burned out. Or washed away, I guess. I just sit there and let it surround me, because what else can I possibly do? If I were afraid, I suppose I would try to run away from it. But like I said, I can barely even get my mouth to form words most days, let alone get up and run. So no... no fear. Just a very, very slow sinking.
Do you believe that the poison in your house is something that only you can see and experience, or do you think others can see it too if they just looked closely enough?

I... I know it sounds far-fetched. Believe me, I can see it in my wife's eyes when I try to explain it to her, how crazy it must sound to someone who isn't trapped in the middle of it. Maybe she just can't see it, or maybe she's refusing to look closely enough because it's just too devastating to accept that our whole life is ruined. But... I am certain. I am absolutely certain that the mold and the wiring in that house have poisoned everything I own. 

It’s not just behind the drywall anymore, doctor. It’s in the fibers of the carpets, it’s soaked into the clothes hanging in my closet, it’s in the important paperwork sitting on the desk that I can't even bring myself to touch. The electrical wiring is just... it's radiating this sickness, baking the mold right into the foundation. Every single thing I have ever worked for or cared about is completely contaminated by it. 

And the thing is... even if my wife doesn't see the dark patches spreading on the floor, other people know. They know exactly what's happening. The neighbors, for instance... I can tell the neighbors are watching. I’ll just be standing by the front window, barely peering through the gaps in the blinds because it takes too much energy to even pull them back, and I see them out there. The guy across the street pretending to check his mail for the third time, the woman next door just lingering at the edge of her lawn with her hose... they aren't just going about their day. They're watching me. 

They know the house is sick. They know everything inside it is poisoned, and they're just watching to see when I mess up again. They're waiting for me to completely fall apart, to make some huge, public mistake so they can finally point and say they knew it all along. It’s like they’re keeping a ledger of my failures out there, just waiting for the rot to finally pull me under. So, maybe they don't see the exact same rushing water I see, but they see the ruin. They know the poison is there, and they're just... they're just waiting for it to finally finish me off. It just adds to the weight of it all, you know? Knowing all those eyes are out there, just staring at the house, waiting for the final collapse.
Do you think anyone else can hear the whispers in the walls or see the dark patches on the floor?

Well, that's... that's the thing of it, isn't it? If they could hear it, maybe they would finally understand what I've been trying to tell them. But no. No, I don't think they can. 

My wife certainly doesn't. In fact, that's what finally scared her. It wasn't the house falling apart that terrified her in the end, it was me. She got so incredibly scared because I keep hearing these things, and she just... she hears nothing. I'll be standing there in the hallway, just frozen, because I can hear the water running. It sounds like a river just rushing behind the drywall, washing everything away. And underneath the sound of the water, there are the voices. Men whispering. It's not just a murmur, it's actual men, whispering right there inside the walls, scheming or talking about the ruin, I don't even know. But I stand there listening to them, and I know there is absolutely nobody there. The house is empty except for us. But the whispering just keeps going.

And she'll come out of the bedroom and ask me what I'm doing, why I'm just staring at the blank wall, and when I try to explain about the men in the walls, she just looks at me with this... this absolute horror. Because she can't hear them. 

And it’s the exact same thing with the floor. I’ll be trying to make my way down the hallway—which takes so much effort now, just dragging my feet across the house—and I will see it. This dark, wet patch. It starts small and then I just watch it spreading, creeping right across the hallway floor, soaking into the wood, ruining it. The poison just expanding. And I'll force myself to get down on my hands and knees... which hurts, everything is just so heavy and exhausted... and I will press my hands right onto the floorboards to feel the water. But it's dry. I have checked it so many times. I rub my hands on it, and the wood is completely dry to the touch, but I am staring right at it and I can still see the dark wetness spreading. 

If my wife could see that patch, she’d be throwing towels down, she’d be frantically trying to clean it up like she always does. But she doesn't do anything. She just watches me kneeling on a dry floor, rubbing my hands on nothing, listening to men who aren't there. So no... nobody else hears the whispers or sees the patches. It’s just me. I'm the only one who has to bear the weight of it, the only one who actually knows how deep the rot goes, while everyone else just stands around being terrified of me.
Have you ever had a period of time where these whispers and visions stopped, even if only for a short while?

Well, stopped? I mean... it's more about when they actually started, I suppose. If you're asking if I've always been like this, the answer is no. Absolutely not. Before... before the house problems just kept dragging on and on, month after endless month, and I fell into this depression... I never had any of this happening to me. I was just a normal guy dealing with a bad situation. I never heard men's voices in the walls. I never saw those dark wet patches that weren't actually there, and I certainly didn't think the neighbors were out there on their lawns tracking my every move. None of that. 

All of those things... the whispers, the water, the eyes on me... they only showed up after everything else had already fallen apart inside me. It was after I had already just... stopped caring about my usual life. There was a point where the weight of the house just got to be too much, and I couldn't even bring myself to do the basic things anymore. I'd just sit in that brown recliner, staring at the dust, not caring about my routine, not caring about the things I used to enjoy, just feeling like a complete and utter failure every single day. I'd wake up, and the very first thought in my head was just how useless I was, how I couldn't protect my home or fix anything for my wife. 

And it was only after that... after I was already hollowed out and feeling like a failure day in and day out... that's when the men started whispering in the drywall. It's like they waited until I was completely empty and broken down before they moved in. So, no, they haven't stopped since they started. But there was a time, before the ruin really took hold of me, before I gave up on my life, when my house was just a house. It feels like a lifetime ago now, though. I can barely even remember what it was like to sit in the quiet without the rushing water.
Have you ever had a time when you didn't hear the whispers or see the dark patches for an extended period?

Like I... like I was just saying, my whole life before this was a time without them. I went decades never hearing a single voice in the drywall, never seeing anything that wasn't there. But since they actually started? No. There hasn't been a break at all. 

This... this specific nightmare has been going on for about seven months now. Seven endless, exhausting months. It all really goes back to that winter freeze we had. You know the one, when the temperatures just dropped out of nowhere and everything iced over? It turned the house repairs I was trying to manage into this... this absolute mess that I just couldn't get out from under. I had been trying so hard to fix the place up, doing what a husband is supposed to do, buying the materials, trying to patch things together. But the freeze just shattered the pipes, ruined the work I'd already done, and made the whole project completely impossible. The damage was just everywhere, practically overnight. 

I remember just standing there, looking at all the ruined materials and thinking about the money we'd lost, and I just realized I was completely trapped. I couldn't fix it. I couldn't save us. It was a mess I was never, ever going to be able to clean up. And that’s when that horrible, heavy emptiness really took over, and I couldn't even get out of my recliner anymore. I just sat there, letting the dust settle on me. And then, right on the heels of that failure, the whispering began. The dark patches started spreading across the floorboards. 

So for seven months, ever since that freeze destroyed what was left of the house and my ability to fix it, it’s been constant. Every single day for seven months, I have to listen to them in the walls. I have to see the rot spreading. There hasn't been a single day of peace or quiet since the ice melted. It just goes on and on, day after day, for seven months straight.
Have you ever had a period where the whispers stopped for more than a day?

I know I keep repeating myself, doctor, and I feel like we're maybe going in circles a bit here, but I really need you to understand the timeline of how this all happened. Because no, they haven't stopped for even twenty-four hours since they actually started. 

But like I was trying to explain just a moment ago... before all these house problems just dragged on and on and on, and I fell into this awful, heavy depression... I never, ever dealt with anything like this. I want to be absolutely clear about that. For my entire life up until a few months ago, I never heard voices in the walls. I never saw wet patches on the floor that weren't actually there. I never spent my days thinking the neighbors were out on their lawns tracking my movements or watching me fail. None of that was part of my life. I was just a normal man trying to take care of his home. 

But those things... the whispers, the water, the feeling of being watched... they didn't just appear out of nowhere. They only showed up after I had already completely given up. It was after I had stopped caring about my usual life, stopped doing anything but sitting in that dusty recliner, just feeling like an absolute, worthless failure every single day. The failure came first, you see? The giving up came first. It was like I was just so hollowed out by the fact that I couldn't fix the house or provide for my wife, that I left the door wide open for all this other stuff to come in. I was too exhausted to care anymore, and that's when the whispers and the rot just walked right into my head. 

So if you're asking if I ever had a day without them recently? No. Not one single day. It is constant. But before the house broke me and I stopped caring about my life? I had decades without them. Decades where it was just quiet.
Did you ever hear voices or see things that weren't there before these whispers in the walls started?

Doctor, I... I really don't know how else to explain this to you. I feel like I'm just repeating the exact same words over and over, and maybe I'm just not making myself clear, but I've said this. No. Never. 

Before the house problems dragged on for all those endless months and I fell into this heavy, awful depression, I never heard voices in the walls. I never saw wet patches on the floor that weren't there, and I never, ever thought the neighbors were tracking me. None of that. It just wasn't part of my life. I was just a normal man, trying to get by and take care of his wife. 

I really need you to understand the order of how this happened, because it feels like you're looking for something that just isn't there. Those things... the whispers, the water, the feeling of being watched... they only showed up after I had already stopped caring about my usual life. They came after I was already spending every single waking moment sitting in that dusty recliner, feeling like a complete and utter failure every single day because I couldn't fix the house. The failure came first. The giving up came first. It was like I just broke under the weight of it all, and once I was completely empty, then the men in the walls moved in. But before that? In all the decades before the house fell apart? No. Never once.
Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely happy, energetic, or irritable for an extended time?

No... no, I haven't. I mean, happy? Energetic? I can't even really remember what that feels like anymore, to be honest with you. It's just been this... this heavy, suffocating blanket over everything for so long now. 

I mean, sure, years ago, back when things were normal, when I was actually working on the house and making progress, I'd have good days. You know, you finish putting up some drywall or fixing a leaky pipe, and you step back and you feel... satisfied. You feel like a man who's actually doing his job, taking care of his home, taking care of his wife. I'd have days where I felt good about that, where I had the energy to wake up early, grab a cup of coffee, and just get to work. But it wasn't anything extreme. It wasn't like I was bouncing off the walls or acting crazy or anything like that. It was just... normal life. Normal satisfaction. 

And irritable? Well, I guess anyone gets frustrated when a project doesn't go right, or when you hit your thumb with a hammer, but... not for an extended time. Not like some mood that just took over my whole personality. 

But lately? Since the freeze? Since the house just completely fell apart and the money ran out? There hasn't been a drop of energy or happiness in me.
